ety.text: From earlier iland, from Middle English iland, yland, ylond, from Old English īeġland, from Proto-West Germanic *auwjuland, from Proto-Germanic *awjōlandą (from Proto-Germanic *awjō (“island, waterland, meadow”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ekʷeh₂) + *landą (“land”), equivalent to ey + land. Doublet of Öland.

senses.d: A contiguous area of land, smaller than a continent, totally surrounded by water.
ex: No man is an Iland, intire of it ſelfe; euery man is a peece of the Continent, a part of the maine; […]
It's only an island if you look at it from the water…

senses.d: A contiguous area of land, smaller than a continent, partially surrounded by water; a peninsula; a half-island.
ex: Despite its name, Barry Island is actually a peninsula

senses.d: An entity surrounded by other entities that are very different from itself.
ex: The quiet library was an island of tranquility in the noisy, bustling city.
an island of colors on a butterfly's wing

senses.d: A superstructure on an aircraft carrier's deck.

ex: the island in the middle of a roundabout
Dunton island, near Birmingham, is one of the most confusingly labelled islands in the U.K.
In Coventry, you will often hear people say: “Turn right at the island”.

senses.d: A bench, counter, etc., that is not connected to a wall or other furniture and which can be used from any side.
ex: A short, rather studious young woman on noticing him moved from behind an island counter.

senses.d: An unincorporated area wholly surrounded by one or more incorporated areas.
A phrase from which a wh-word cannot be extracted without yielding invalid grammar.
ex: Adverbial subordinate clauses are islands for extraction: "They have a billion dollars of inventory that they don't know where *(it) is".

senses.d: To surround with water; make into an island.
ex: The car soon seemed islanded in water.

senses.d: To set, dot (as if) with islands.

ex: High the vanes of Shrewsbury gleam / Islanded in Severn stream.

ety.text: Originally written isle; from Middle French isle, from Old French isle, from Vulgar Latin *īsula, from Classical Latin īnsula.
From Vulgar Latin *isula, from classical Latin īnsula.

es:isla.gl: island (area of land surrounded by water)

ety.text: Inherited from Old Spanish isla, from Vulgar Latin *īsula, from Latin īnsula (compare Catalan illa, French île, Galician insua, Italian isola, Portuguese ínsua). Doublet of ínsula, a borrowing. Cognate with English isle but false cognate of English island.

From Old Galician-Portuguese illa, from Old Catalan illa, from Vulgar Latin *īsula, from Latin īnsula, whence also Spanish isla, Italian isola, French île and English isle. Doublet of inherited ínsua, from Old Galician-Portuguese inssoa, as well as the learned borrowing ínsula; both of these are rare or specialist.
Borrowed from Late Latin Oasis (“name of various oases”), from Ancient Greek Ὄασις (Óasis), from Demotic Egyptian wḥj, from Egyptian wḥꜣt (“oasis, cauldron”), G43-V28-G1-X1:N25.

pt:ilhar.gl: to isolate (to cut off from others)

ety.text: From ilha + -ar. Piecewise doublet of insular (verb) and isolar.
From Latin īnsulātus, from īnsulāre, from īnsula (“island”). Equivalent to isola + -àre.
Italian isolatobor. French isolébf. French isolerbor. Portuguese isolar Borrowed from French isoler. Piecewise doublet of ilhar and insular (verb).
